stimuli.description: Eleven different material samples (6 original building materials: blue stone, brickwork, concrete, white plaster, steel, wood; and 5 colored plaster samples equivalent in color to original materials) presented vertically at eye-height.

tables.description: Overview of the thermal properties and technical measurements of the test samples (thermal conductivity k, specific heat c, density p, thermal effusivity η, average roughness Ra, mean square roughness Rq, gloss (60°/85°), lightness L*, red-green value a*, yellow-blue value b*, color intensity I*).
Pearson correlation coefficients between evaluated material warmth and physical measures in the three experimental conditions (General, Visual, Tactile).

limitations: The variety of materials allowed for a broad perspective on the concept of material warmth, but did not allow to formulate detailed findings concerning the exact relationships between material warmth and the technical material parameters.

In order to generalize these findings, the material set would have to be expanded to a larger number of different samples and the researched variables (thermal properties, surface roughness, gloss) should be controlled.
The sample set was not chosen to cover a wide variety of colors, requiring more detailed investigation utilizing a more complete color set.

The study focused on indoor wall materials; warmth perception is likely to be context-dependent, so results should be considered within the boundary conditions set for the test. Applications for other building elements (floors, ceilings, outdoor applications) require further research.

Participants were asked to imagine the materials at full scale but their ability to do so might be limited, suggesting that studies in full-scale settings might provide insights into differences in perception caused by issues of scale.
